```{r helpers}
# Helper functions used throughout Task 1. Function names follow Google's
# R Style Guide (BigCamelCase); objects use snake_case.

# Convert text to numbers, tolerating thousands separators, currency
# symbols, stray spaces and the Unicode minus sign. Anything that still is
# not a number becomes NA, so it can be counted as a defect.
ToNumber <- function(x) {
  x <- str_replace_all(as.character(x), "−", "-")
  x <- str_remove_all(x, "[,$\\s]")
  suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))
}

# Label each Year value by its format, so the variants can be reported.
ClassifyYearFormat <- function(x) {
  x <- str_trim(as.character(x))
  case_when(
    is.na(x) | x == "" ~ "missing",
    str_detect(x, "^\\d{4}$") ~ "YYYY",
    str_detect(x, "^\\d{4}\\.0+$") ~ "YYYY.0 (decimal)",
    str_detect(x, "^\\d{4}-\\d{1,2}-\\d{1,2}") ~ "ISO date (YYYY-MM-DD)",
    str_detect(x, "^\\d{1,2}[/.-]\\d{1,2}[/.-]\\d{4}$") ~ "D/M/YYYY date",
    str_detect(x, "^\\d{5}$") ~ "Excel serial number",
    str_detect(x, "^'?\\d{2}$") ~ "two-digit year",
    str_detect(x, "[A-Za-z]") & str_detect(x, "\\d{4}") ~ "text + year",
    TRUE ~ "other"
  )
}

# Convert every Year variant to a four-digit integer year.
ParseYear <- function(x) {
  x <- str_trim(as.character(x))
  fmt <- ClassifyYearFormat(x)
  out <- rep(NA_integer_, length(x))

  idx <- fmt %in% c("YYYY", "YYYY.0 (decimal)", "ISO date (YYYY-MM-DD)")
  out[idx] <- as.integer(str_sub(x[idx], 1, 4))

  idx <- fmt == "D/M/YYYY date"
  out[idx] <- year(parse_date_time(x[idx], orders = c("dmy", "mdy")))

  idx <- fmt == "Excel serial number"
  out[idx] <- year(as_date(as.numeric(x[idx]), origin = "1899-12-30"))

  idx <- fmt == "two-digit year"
  yy <- as.integer(str_remove(x[idx], "'"))
  out[idx] <- if_else(yy > 50L, 1900L + yy, 2000L + yy)

  idx <- fmt == "text + year"
  out[idx] <- as.integer(str_extract(x[idx], "(19|20)\\d{2}"))

  idx <- fmt == "other"
  out[idx] <- year(parse_date_time(x[idx],
                                   orders = c("Ymd", "dmY", "mdY", "bY")))
  out
}

# Normalise country names so the same country matches across files
# (case, accents, punctuation, "&", leading "The").
NormaliseName <- function(x) {
  x %>%
    iconv(to = "ASCII//TRANSLIT", sub = "") %>%
    str_to_lower() %>%
    str_replace_all("&", "and") %>%
    str_remove_all("[^a-z0-9 ]") %>%
    str_remove("^the ") %>%
    str_squish()
}

# Known spelling variants (normalised alias = normalised canonical name).
# DECISION: extend this list with any names printed as "Unmatched name -
# review" in Task 1.2.
name_fixes <- c(
  "united states of america" = "united states",
  "usa" = "united states",
  "us" = "united states",
  "russian federation" = "russia",
  "korea rep" = "south korea",
  "republic of korea" = "south korea",
  "viet nam" = "vietnam",
  "czech republic" = "czechia",
  "turkiye" = "turkey",
  "iran islamic rep" = "iran",
  "egypt arab rep" = "egypt",
  "uk" = "united kingdom",
  "slovak republic" = "slovakia",
  "kyrgyz republic" = "kyrgyzstan",
  "lao pdr" = "laos",
  "dr congo" = "democratic republic of congo",
  "congo dem rep" = "democratic republic of congo",
  "congo rep" = "congo",
  "ivory coast" = "cote divoire",
  "burma" = "myanmar",
  "syrian arab republic" = "syria",
  "venezuela bolivarian republic of" = "venezuela"
)

ApplyNameFixes <- function(key) {
  if_else(key %in% names(name_fixes), unname(name_fixes[key]), key)
}

# Linear interpolation within one country's series. End gaps take the
# nearest observed value (rule = 2). A series with a single observation is
# filled with that value; an all-NA series is returned unchanged.
InterpolateWithin <- function(year, value) {
  ok <- !is.na(value)
  if (sum(ok) == 0) return(value)
  if (sum(ok) == 1) return(replace(value, !ok, value[ok]))
  approx(year[ok], value[ok], xout = year, rule = 2)$y
}

# Flag values more than `multiple` times above (or below) the country's
# own median: the signature of a unit or keying error (e.g. x1000).
FlagSpikes <- function(value, multiple = 10) {
  med <- median(value[value > 0], na.rm = TRUE)
  if (is.na(med)) return(rep(FALSE, length(value)))
  high <- value > multiple * med
  low <- med > 1 & value > 0 & value < med / multiple
  replace(high | low, is.na(high | low), FALSE)
}

# Most frequent non-missing value (NA if there is none).
ModeValue <- function(x) {
  counts <- table(x)
  if (length(counts) == 0) return(NA_character_)
  names(sort(counts, decreasing = TRUE))[1]
}

# A readable "Country Year" label for example rows in the audit table.
LabelRows <- function(df) {
  id <- if ("Country" %in% names(df)) df$Country else df$ISO
  if ("Year" %in% names(df)) paste(id, df$Year) else as.character(id)
}

# Defect log: every detection step below appends a row, which becomes the
# Data Quality Audit table in Task 1A.
defect_log <- tibble(
  File = character(), Column = character(), Rows = integer(),
  Example = character(), Detection = character(), Handling = character()
)

LogDefect <- function(log, file, column, rows_df, detection, handling) {
  examples <- if (nrow(rows_df) == 0) "-" else
    paste(head(unique(LabelRows(rows_df)), 2), collapse = "; ")
  add_row(log, File = file, Column = column, Rows = nrow(rows_df),
          Example = examples, Detection = detection, Handling = handling)
}

# Codes sometimes used for "missing" in place of NA.
sentinel_values <- c(-999, -9999, -99999, 99999, 999999)

# Model evaluation metrics (Task 3).
Rmse <- function(actual, predicted) sqrt(mean((actual - predicted)^2))
RSquared <- function(actual, predicted) {
  1 - sum((actual - predicted)^2) / sum((actual - mean(actual))^2)
}
```

# Introduction

Understanding which countries are responsible for carbon dioxide
emissions, and how that responsibility should be measured, is central
to climate policy. This report examines national CO2 emissions and
renewable electricity generation using data from Our World in Data's
CO2 and energy datasets, which compile figures from the Global Carbon
Project, Ember, the Energy Institute and the World Bank. Although the
underlying values are genuine, the slice analysed here is personalised
from my student ID: it covers 150 countries across six regions over the
period 2004–2023 and arrives as four deliberately imperfect files. The
master panel, \`Emissions.csv\`, records annual production-based CO2 and
oil CO2 for each country; \`Renewables.csv\` reports renewable
generation
in a wide, name-keyed format; \`Consumption.csv\` provides
trade-adjusted,
consumption-based emissions for a subset of countries; and
\`Countries.csv\` supplies static 2022 population and GDP figures. The
files differ in shape, key structure and coverage, and each contains
undisclosed data-quality defects, so preparing them for analysis is a
substantial task in its own right.

The analysis is guided by four objectives. The first is to detect,
document and defensibly repair those defects so that the four sources
can be merged into a single tidy country-year panel. The second is to
explore which countries and regions account for the largest share of
emissions, and how rankings shift between total, per-capita and
consumption-based measures. The third is to assess how well a country's
cumulative emissions can be predicted from its economic and demographic
characteristics, and whether the assumptions underlying linear
regression hold for these data. The fourth is to translate these
findings into a dashboard design that communicates the energy
transition to a public audience.

The work is carried out in R using a small set of established packages.
The \`tidyverse\` provides the core tools for importing, reshaping and
summarising data (\`readr\`, \`tidyr\`, \`dplyr\` and \`stringr\`) and
for
visualisation (\`ggplot2\`); \`lubridate\` parses the inconsistent year
formats found in the source files; \`scales\` formats axis labels and
logarithmic scales; \`knitr\` renders tables; and \`glmnet\` and
\`rpart\`
implement the ridge, lasso and regression-tree models used to extend the
linear analysis.

The anticipated outcome is a fully reproducible analysis: a cleaned
master data frame in which every defect is logged alongside its method
of detection and its treatment; a set of rankings and visualisations
that distinguish countries that emit the most in total from those that
emit most intensively; regression models evaluated on a held-out test
set, with their assumptions examined and their limitations made
explicit; and a dashboard design grounded in these results.

The report is organised to follow these objectives. Task 1 imports,
cleans, merges and extends the data, followed by a Data Quality Audit
(1A). Task 2 explores the cleaned data, including a counterintuitive
finding (2A) and a critique of one visualisation (2B). Task 3 develops
and evaluates the predictive models, examines their assumptions (3A) and
critiques the choice of predictor (3B). Task 4 presents the dashboard
design, and the report concludes with a summary of findings, a
verification table, a reproducibility appendix and a Decision Log.

## Assumptions

1.  **Emissions.csv defines the country set.** It is the master panel,
    so its 150 countries and its 2004–2023 window define the scope.
    Totals describe this sample, not the whole world; Australia, for
    example, is not among my 150 countries.
2.  **Units are consistent across years and countries:** emissions in
    million tonnes of CO2 (Mt), renewables in terawatt-hours (TWh), GDP
    in millions of international dollars and GDP per capita in
    international dollars.
3.  **`annual_co2_mt` is production-based fossil CO2.** It records
    emissions inside a country's borders and contains no land-use sinks,
    so a negative value is treated as an error, not a removal.
4.  **Static country data apply to every year.** `Countries.csv` holds a
    single 2022 value per country, so per-capita measures divide
    cumulative totals by 2022 population.
5.  **"Cumulative" means cumulative within the window.** `CumCO2` and
    the other running totals start from 2004, not from a country's first
    historical emissions.
6.  **Missing is not zero.** A missing value is filled from the same
    country's neighbouring years where possible; a country with no
    consumption data is assumed trade-neutral (`ConsCO2 = CO2`).
7.  **Aggregate rows are not countries.** Rows such as "World" or
    "European Union (27)" duplicate the countries they contain and are
    excluded.
8.  **The Paris split follows the brief.** "Pre-Paris" covers years
    before 2016 and "Post-Paris" 2016 onwards (the agreement was adopted
    in December 2015).

# Task 1: Data preparation and wrangling

### 1.1 Import the four CSV files

```{r t1q1}
# Everything is read as text first. Numbers stored as text, odd Year
# formats and stray whitespace would otherwise be coerced silently, and the
# defects would be lost before they could be counted.
ReadRaw <- function(path) {
  read_csv(path, col_types = cols(.default = col_character()),
           na = c("", "NA"), trim_ws = FALSE)
}

emissions_raw   <- ReadRaw("data/Emissions.csv")
renewables_raw  <- ReadRaw("data/Renewables.csv")
consumption_raw <- ReadRaw("data/Consumption.csv")
countries_raw   <- ReadRaw("data/Countries.csv")

raw_files <- list(Emissions = emissions_raw, Renewables = renewables_raw,
                  Consumption = consumption_raw, Countries = countries_raw)

tibble(File = names(raw_files),
       Rows = map_int(raw_files, nrow),
       Columns = map_int(raw_files, ncol),
       ColumnNames = map_chr(raw_files, ~ paste(head(names(.x), 6),
                                                collapse = ", "))) %>%
  kable(caption = "Raw files as imported")
```

### 1.2 Reshape `Renewables.csv` to one row per country per year

*Remember: this file contains rows that are not countries.*

```{r t1q2}
# Year columns are any whose name contains a four-digit number
# (e.g. "2010", "X2010"); the remaining column(s) identify the row.
year_cols <- names(renewables_raw)[str_detect(names(renewables_raw),
                                              "\\d{4}")]
id_cols <- setdiff(names(renewables_raw), year_cols)
cat("Identifier column(s):", paste(id_cols, collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("Year columns:", length(year_cols), "\n")

# Wide -> long: one row per country per year. Year stays as text here and
# is standardised in 1.4 together with the other files.
renewables_long <- renewables_raw %>%
  rename(Country = all_of(id_cols[1])) %>%
  pivot_longer(all_of(year_cols), names_to = "Year",
               values_to = "Renewables") %>%
  mutate(Country = str_squish(Country),
         NameKey = ApplyNameFixes(NormaliseName(Country)))

# Renewables.csv has no ISO code, so names are mapped to ISO codes using
# the names in Emissions.csv and Countries.csv.
name_lookup <- bind_rows(
  emissions_raw %>%
    transmute(ISO = str_to_upper(str_trim(iso_code)), Name = location),
  countries_raw %>%
    transmute(ISO = str_to_upper(str_trim(countryCode)), Name = Country)
) %>%
  filter(str_detect(ISO, "^[A-Z]{3}$")) %>%
  mutate(NameKey = ApplyNameFixes(NormaliseName(Name))) %>%
  distinct(NameKey, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  select(NameKey, ISO)

renewables_long <- renewables_long %>%
  left_join(name_lookup, by = "NameKey")

# Rows whose name matches no country are either aggregates (World,
# continents, income groups, "(EI)"-style source regions) or spelling
# variants that still need adding to name_fixes.
aggregate_pattern <- paste0(
  "world|income|oecd|union|\\(|total|other|non-|^africa|^asia|^europe|",
  "america|oceania|middle east|cis|ussr|g20|g7|opec|pacific|caribbean|",
  "eurasia|region"
)

renew_non_country <- renewables_long %>%
  filter(is.na(ISO)) %>%
  distinct(Country) %>%
  mutate(Type = if_else(str_detect(str_to_lower(Country), aggregate_pattern),
                        "Aggregate / region",
                        "Unmatched name - review"))

kable(count(renew_non_country, Type),
      caption = "Renewables.csv rows that are not countries")
print(renew_non_country, n = Inf)

defect_log <- LogDefect(
  defect_log, "Renewables.csv", "Country",
  renewables_long %>% filter(is.na(ISO)),
  paste("Names with no match in the Emissions/Countries name lookup",
        "after normalisation; classified by keyword"),
  "Removed (aggregates double-count countries already in the data)"
)

# DECISION: drop every row that does not map to a country ISO code.
renewables_long <- renewables_long %>%
  filter(!is.na(ISO)) %>%
  select(ISO, Country, Year, Renewables)
```

*What did you do with the non-country rows, and why?*

Renewables.csv identifies each row by name only (\`Country.Region\`),
with one column per year from 2004 to 2023. After pivoting it to one row
per country per year, I mapped each name to an ISO code using the
country names in Emissions.csv and Countries.csv. Names were normalised
(case, accents, punctuation) and known spelling variants were corrected
first, such as "United States of America" for "United States". Every row
matched a country except two: "World" and "European Union (27)".

I removed both rows, which is 40 country-year observations (2 rows × 20
years). They are not countries but aggregates: "World" is the sum of
every country's generation, and "European Union (27)" is the sum of its
27 member states, several of which (e.g. France, Germany, Italy) already
appear as individual rows. Keeping them would break the
one-country-per-year structure of the master data frame. They would also
double-count renewable generation when totals are summed across
countries in Task 2. They also have no ISO code, so they could not be
joined to Emissions.csv.

### 1.3 Rename the columns

```{r t1q3}
emissions <- emissions_raw %>%
  rename(ISO = iso_code, Country = location, Region = region,
         Year = year, CO2 = annual_co2_mt, OilCO2 = annual_oil_co2_mt)

consumption <- consumption_raw %>%
  rename(ISO = `Country Code`, ConsCO2 = `Consumption CO2`)

countries <- countries_raw %>%
  rename(ISO = countryCode, Population = popData2022,
         GDPCapita = `GDP/capita`)

# --- Type conversion, with defect detection before each change ----------

# ISO codes with whitespace or lower case break joins silently.
for (name in c("emissions", "consumption", "countries")) {
  df <- get(name)
  bad_iso <- df %>%
    filter(!is.na(ISO), !str_detect(ISO, "^[A-Z]{3}$"),
           str_detect(str_to_upper(str_trim(ISO)), "^[A-Z]{3}$"))
  file <- paste0(str_to_title(name), ".csv")
  defect_log <- LogDefect(
    defect_log, file, "ISO", bad_iso,
    paste("Failed the three-capital-letter regex but passed after",
          "str_trim() and str_to_upper()"),
    "Trimmed and upper-cased"
  )
}

# Values that are present but not numeric (e.g. "n/a", "unknown").
numeric_targets <- list(
  list("emissions", "Emissions.csv", c("CO2", "OilCO2")),
  list("consumption", "Consumption.csv", "ConsCO2"),
  list("countries", "Countries.csv", c("Population", "GDP", "GDPCapita")),
  list("renewables_long", "Renewables.csv", "Renewables")
)

for (target in numeric_targets) {
  df <- get(target[[1]])
  for (col in target[[3]]) {
    non_numeric <- df[!is.na(df[[col]]) & is.na(ToNumber(df[[col]])), ]
    defect_log <- LogDefect(
      defect_log, target[[2]], col, non_numeric,
      "Non-missing text that ToNumber() could not convert to a number",
      "Set to NA, then treated in Task 1.6"
    )
  }
}

# Numbers written with thousands separators (e.g. "9,443.433") are read
# as text; ToNumber() repairs them, but they are a formatting defect.
for (target in numeric_targets) {
  df <- get(target[[1]])
  for (col in target[[3]]) {
    comma_rows <- df[!is.na(df[[col]]) & str_detect(df[[col]], ","), ]
    defect_log <- LogDefect(
      defect_log, target[[2]], col, comma_rows,
      "str_detect(value, \",\"): thousands separator stored as text",
      "Separator removed by ToNumber() before conversion"
    )
  }
}

# Region labels with inconsistent spacing or case.
region_variants <- emissions %>%
  filter(!is.na(Region), Region != str_to_title(str_squish(Region)))
defect_log <- LogDefect(
  defect_log, "Emissions.csv", "Region", region_variants,
  "table(Region) showed the same continent spelt in more than one way",
  "str_squish() + str_to_title(), then each country's most common label"
)

# Now convert.
emissions <- emissions %>%
  mutate(ISO = str_to_upper(str_trim(ISO)),
         Country = str_squish(Country),
         Region = str_to_title(str_squish(Region)),
         across(c(CO2, OilCO2), ToNumber))

consumption <- consumption %>%
  mutate(ISO = str_to_upper(str_trim(ISO)), ConsCO2 = ToNumber(ConsCO2))

countries <- countries %>%
  mutate(ISO = str_to_upper(str_trim(ISO)),
         Country = str_squish(Country),
         across(c(Population, GDP, GDPCapita), ToNumber))

renewables_long <- renewables_long %>%
  mutate(Renewables = ToNumber(Renewables))

map(list(Emissions = emissions, Consumption = consumption,
         Countries = countries, Renewables = renewables_long), names)
```

### 1.4 Make `Year` consistent across all data frames

```{r t1q4}
# Detection: which Year formats appear in each file?
year_formats <- bind_rows(
  tibble(File = "Emissions.csv", Format = ClassifyYearFormat(emissions$Year)),
  tibble(File = "Consumption.csv",
         Format = ClassifyYearFormat(consumption$Year)),
  tibble(File = "Renewables.csv (column names)",
         Format = ClassifyYearFormat(renewables_long$Year))
)
year_formats %>%
  count(File, Format) %>%
  kable(caption = "Year formats found in each file")

for (name in c("emissions", "consumption")) {
  df <- get(name)
  odd <- df %>% filter(ClassifyYearFormat(Year) != "YYYY")
  defect_log <- LogDefect(
    defect_log, paste0(str_to_title(name), ".csv"), "Year", odd,
    "ClassifyYearFormat() found values not in plain YYYY form",
    "Converted to integer year with ParseYear() (lubridate for dates)"
  )
}

# Convert every Year to the same type: a four-digit integer.
emissions <- emissions %>% mutate(Year = ParseYear(Year))
consumption <- consumption %>% mutate(Year = ParseYear(Year))
renewables_long <- renewables_long %>% mutate(Year = ParseYear(Year))

# Check: same class everywhere, and no values that failed to parse.
tibble(
  Frame = c("emissions", "consumption", "renewables_long"),
  Class = c(class(emissions$Year), class(consumption$Year),
            class(renewables_long$Year)),
  Unparsed = c(sum(is.na(emissions$Year)), sum(is.na(consumption$Year)),
               sum(is.na(renewables_long$Year))),
  Range = c(paste(range(emissions$Year, na.rm = TRUE), collapse = "-"),
            paste(range(consumption$Year, na.rm = TRUE), collapse = "-"),
            paste(range(renewables_long$Year, na.rm = TRUE),
                  collapse = "-"))
) %>%
  kable(caption = "Year after standardisation")

# Rows whose Year could not be recovered cannot be placed in time.
emissions <- filter(emissions, !is.na(Year))
consumption <- filter(consumption, !is.na(Year))
renewables_long <- filter(renewables_long, !is.na(Year))
```

### 1.4b Remove non-country rows, duplicates and impossible values

```{r t1-clean}
# --- Emissions.csv (the master panel) ------------------------------------
n_emissions_raw <- nrow(emissions)

# 1. Non-country rows (aggregates have codes such as OWID_WRL or no code).
emissions_non_country <- emissions %>%
  filter(is.na(ISO) | !str_detect(ISO, "^[A-Z]{3}$"))
defect_log <- LogDefect(
  defect_log, "Emissions.csv", "ISO", emissions_non_country,
  "ISO missing or not three letters (aggregate rows such as OWID_*)",
  "Removed so totals are not double-counted"
)
emissions <- anti_join(emissions, emissions_non_country,
                       by = names(emissions))

# 2. Exact duplicate rows.
n_dup_exact <- nrow(emissions) - nrow(distinct(emissions))
dup_exact_rows <- emissions[duplicated(emissions), ]
emissions <- distinct(emissions)

# 3. Same country and year recorded twice with different values.
dup_key_rows <- emissions %>%
  group_by(ISO, Year) %>%
  filter(n() > 1) %>%
  ungroup()
emissions <- emissions %>%
  arrange(ISO, Year, is.na(CO2)) %>%   # keep the non-missing copy first
  distinct(ISO, Year, .keep_all = TRUE)
n_dup_key <- nrow(dup_key_rows) - n_distinct(dup_key_rows[c("ISO", "Year")])
n_dup_removed <- n_dup_exact + n_dup_key

defect_log <- LogDefect(
  defect_log, "Emissions.csv", "(whole row)", dup_exact_rows,
  "duplicated() on all columns", "Removed with distinct()"
)
defect_log <- LogDefect(
  defect_log, "Emissions.csv", "ISO + Year", dup_key_rows,
  "group_by(ISO, Year) with n() > 1 after exact duplicates removed",
  "Kept the first non-missing record per country-year"
)
cat("Duplicate rows removed:", n_dup_removed,
    "(exact:", n_dup_exact, "| same key:", n_dup_key, ")\n")

# 4. Years outside this student's data window (keying errors).
window_years <- range(as.integer(my$window))
out_of_window <- emissions %>%
  filter(Year < window_years[1] | Year > window_years[2])
defect_log <- LogDefect(
  defect_log, "Emissions.csv", "Year", out_of_window,
  paste0("Year outside the personalised window ",
         window_years[1], "-", window_years[2]),
  "Removed"
)
emissions <- anti_join(emissions, out_of_window, by = c("ISO", "Year"))

# 5. One consistent name and region per country (most common label).
inconsistent_labels <- emissions %>%
  group_by(ISO) %>%
  filter(n_distinct(Country) > 1 | n_distinct(Region, na.rm = TRUE) > 1 |
           any(is.na(Region))) %>%
  ungroup()
defect_log <- LogDefect(
  defect_log, "Emissions.csv", "Country / Region", inconsistent_labels,
  "group_by(ISO) with n_distinct(Country/Region) > 1 or missing Region",
  "Replaced with that country's most frequent label"
)
emissions <- emissions %>%
  group_by(ISO) %>%
  mutate(
    Country = ModeValue(Country),
    Region = ModeValue(Region)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Keep an untouched copy of the values for the audit (1A).
emissions_before_fix <- emissions

# 6. Missing-value codes such as -999.
sentinel_rows <- emissions %>%
  filter(CO2 %in% sentinel_values | OilCO2 %in% sentinel_values)
defect_log <- LogDefect(
  defect_log, "Emissions.csv", "CO2 / OilCO2", sentinel_rows,
  "Exact matches to codes like -999 / 99999",
  "Treated as missing (NA), interpolated in Task 1.6"
)
emissions <- emissions %>%
  mutate(across(c(CO2, OilCO2), ~ if_else(.x %in% sentinel_values,
                                          NA_real_, .x)))

# 7. Negative annual emissions (Task 1A ii).
negative_rows <- emissions %>%
  filter(CO2 < 0) %>%
  select(ISO, Country, Year, CO2)
defect_log <- LogDefect(
  defect_log, "Emissions.csv", "CO2", negative_rows,
  "summary(CO2) showed a negative minimum; filter(CO2 < 0)",
  "Set to NA and interpolated from neighbouring years (Task 1.6)"
)
neg_oil <- emissions %>% filter(OilCO2 < 0)
defect_log <- LogDefect(
  defect_log, "Emissions.csv", "OilCO2", neg_oil,
  "filter(OilCO2 < 0)", "Set to NA and interpolated (Task 1.6)"
)
# DECISION: negative values become NA and are interpolated, not set to 0.
emissions <- emissions %>%
  mutate(CO2 = if_else(CO2 < 0, NA_real_, CO2),
         OilCO2 = if_else(OilCO2 < 0, NA_real_, OilCO2))

# 8. Spikes: a value 10x away from the country's own median.
emissions <- emissions %>%
  group_by(ISO) %>%
  mutate(CO2Spike = FlagSpikes(CO2), OilSpike = FlagSpikes(OilCO2)) %>%
  ungroup()
spike_rows <- emissions %>% filter(CO2Spike | OilSpike)
defect_log <- LogDefect(
  defect_log, "Emissions.csv", "CO2 / OilCO2", spike_rows,
  "Value more than 10x above/below the country's own median (FlagSpikes)",
  "Set to NA and interpolated (likely unit or keying error)"
)
emissions <- emissions %>%
  mutate(CO2 = if_else(CO2Spike, NA_real_, CO2),
         OilCO2 = if_else(OilSpike, NA_real_, OilCO2)) %>%
  select(-CO2Spike, -OilSpike)

# 9. Oil emissions larger than total emissions (logically impossible).
oil_gt_total <- emissions %>% filter(OilCO2 > CO2)
defect_log <- LogDefect(
  defect_log, "Emissions.csv", "OilCO2", oil_gt_total,
  "filter(OilCO2 > CO2): a component cannot exceed its total",
  "OilCO2 set to NA and interpolated"
)
emissions <- emissions %>%
  mutate(OilCO2 = if_else(!is.na(CO2) & OilCO2 > CO2, NA_real_, OilCO2))

# 10. Missing years inside a country's record (reported, not filled).
year_gaps <- emissions %>%
  group_by(ISO, Country) %>%
  summarise(YearsPresent = n(),
            YearsExpected = max(Year) - min(Year) + 1, .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(YearsPresent < YearsExpected)
cat("Countries with missing years inside their record:", nrow(year_gaps),
    "\n")

# --- Consumption.csv -----------------------------------------------------
cons_dups <- consumption %>% group_by(ISO, Year) %>% filter(n() > 1) %>%
  ungroup()
defect_log <- LogDefect(
  defect_log, "Consumption.csv", "ISO + Year", cons_dups,
  "group_by(ISO, Year) with n() > 1", "Kept first non-missing record"
)
consumption <- consumption %>%
  arrange(ISO, Year, is.na(ConsCO2)) %>%
  distinct(ISO, Year, .keep_all = TRUE)

cons_bad <- consumption %>%
  filter(ConsCO2 %in% sentinel_values | ConsCO2 < 0)
defect_log <- LogDefect(
  defect_log, "Consumption.csv", "ConsCO2", cons_bad,
  "Missing-value codes or negative values (filter(ConsCO2 < 0))",
  "Set to NA and interpolated (Task 1.6)"
)
consumption <- consumption %>%
  mutate(ConsCO2 = if_else(ConsCO2 %in% sentinel_values | ConsCO2 < 0,
                           NA_real_, ConsCO2)) %>%
  group_by(ISO) %>%
  mutate(Spike = FlagSpikes(ConsCO2)) %>%
  ungroup()
defect_log <- LogDefect(
  defect_log, "Consumption.csv", "ConsCO2", filter(consumption, Spike),
  "Value more than 10x from the country's own median (FlagSpikes)",
  "Set to NA and interpolated"
)
consumption <- consumption %>%
  mutate(ConsCO2 = if_else(Spike, NA_real_, ConsCO2)) %>%
  select(-Spike)

# --- Countries.csv -------------------------------------------------------
ctry_dups <- countries %>% group_by(ISO) %>% filter(n() > 1) %>% ungroup()
defect_log <- LogDefect(
  defect_log, "Countries.csv", "ISO", ctry_dups,
  "group_by(ISO) with n() > 1 in a one-row-per-country table",
  "Kept the most complete record"
)
countries <- countries %>%
  arrange(ISO, is.na(Population) + is.na(GDP) + is.na(GDPCapita)) %>%
  distinct(ISO, .keep_all = TRUE)

ctry_bad <- countries %>%
  filter(Population <= 0 | GDP <= 0 | GDPCapita <= 0 |
           Population %in% sentinel_values | GDP %in% sentinel_values)
defect_log <- LogDefect(
  defect_log, "Countries.csv", "Population / GDP / GDPCapita", ctry_bad,
  "summary() showed zero/negative minima or missing-value codes",
  "Set to NA, then derived or imputed in Task 1.6"
)
countries <- countries %>%
  mutate(across(c(Population, GDP, GDPCapita),
                ~ if_else(.x <= 0 | .x %in% sentinel_values,
                          NA_real_, .x)))

# The three columns are linked: GDP (millions) * 1e6 / Population should
# reproduce GDPCapita. When they disagree, the population implied by GDP
# and GDPCapita shows whether Population is the value that is wrong.
ctry_inconsistent <- countries %>%
  mutate(ImpliedPopulation = GDP * 1e6 / GDPCapita,
         Ratio = Population / ImpliedPopulation) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Ratio), abs(Ratio - 1) > 0.05)
print(select(ctry_inconsistent, ISO, Country, Population, GDP, GDPCapita,
             ImpliedPopulation, Ratio))
defect_log <- LogDefect(
  defect_log, "Countries.csv", "Population", ctry_inconsistent,
  paste("Population differs >5% from GDP * 1e6 / GDPCapita",
        "(ratio printed above)"),
  "Replaced with the population implied by GDP and GDPCapita"
)
# DECISION: GDP and GDPCapita agree with each other, so Population is the
# inconsistent value; replace it with the implied population.
countries <- countries %>%
  mutate(Population = if_else(ISO %in% ctry_inconsistent$ISO,
                              round(GDP * 1e6 / GDPCapita), Population))

# --- Renewables ----------------------------------------------------------
renew_dups <- renewables_long %>% group_by(ISO, Year) %>%
  filter(n() > 1) %>% ungroup()
defect_log <- LogDefect(
  defect_log, "Renewables.csv", "Country + Year", renew_dups,
  "Two name variants mapped to the same ISO and year",
  "Kept the first non-missing value"
)
renewables_long <- renewables_long %>%
  arrange(ISO, Year, is.na(Renewables)) %>%
  distinct(ISO, Year, .keep_all = TRUE)

renew_bad <- renewables_long %>%
  filter(Renewables < 0 | Renewables %in% sentinel_values)
defect_log <- LogDefect(
  defect_log, "Renewables.csv", "Renewables", renew_bad,
  "Negative generation or missing-value codes",
  "Set to NA and interpolated (Task 1.6)"
)
renewables_long <- renewables_long %>%
  mutate(Renewables = if_else(Renewables < 0 |
                                Renewables %in% sentinel_values,
                              NA_real_, Renewables))

# Blank cells inside the wide table (missing years for a country).
renew_blank <- renewables_long %>% filter(is.na(Renewables))
defect_log <- LogDefect(
  defect_log, "Renewables.csv", "Renewables", renew_blank,
  "is.na(Renewables) after pivoting: empty cells in the wide table",
  "Interpolated from neighbouring years (Task 1.6)"
)
# DECISION: no spike check on renewables. Generation that grows from
# near zero (e.g. new solar programmes) legitimately exceeds 10x its
# median, so FlagSpikes() would remove real growth.

cat("Emissions rows: ", n_emissions_raw, "->", nrow(emissions), "\n")
n_countries <- n_distinct(emissions$ISO)
cat("Countries in Emissions.csv:", n_countries, "\n")
```

### 1.5 Merge the five new variables into the master data frame

*Add `Renewables`, `ConsCO2`, `Population`, `GDP`, `GDPCapita`.*

```{r t1q5}
# Emissions is the master: left joins keep every country-year in it.
# Each source gets a match flag so a genuine NA value can be told apart
# from a row that failed to join.
#   Renewables  -> ISO + Year (ISO obtained from the country name in 1.2)
#   Consumption -> ISO + Year
#   Countries   -> ISO only (static 2022 reference values)
master <- emissions %>%
  left_join(renewables_long %>%
              select(ISO, Year, Renewables) %>%
              mutate(RenewMatch = TRUE),
            by = c("ISO", "Year")) %>%
  left_join(consumption %>%
              select(ISO, Year, ConsCO2) %>%
              mutate(ConsMatch = TRUE),
            by = c("ISO", "Year")) %>%
  left_join(countries %>%
              select(ISO, Population, GDP, GDPCapita) %>%
              mutate(CtryMatch = TRUE),
            by = "ISO")

# A left join must never add rows to the master.
stopifnot(nrow(master) == nrow(emissions))

join_report <- tibble(
  Join = c("Renewables (name -> ISO, + Year)", "Consumption (ISO + Year)",
           "Countries (ISO)"),
  MasterRowsUnmatched = c(sum(is.na(master$RenewMatch)),
                          sum(is.na(master$ConsMatch)),
                          sum(is.na(master$CtryMatch))),
  CountriesUnmatched = c(n_distinct(master$ISO[is.na(master$RenewMatch)]),
                         n_distinct(master$ISO[is.na(master$ConsMatch)]),
                         n_distinct(master$ISO[is.na(master$CtryMatch)])),
  SourceRowsUnused = c(
    nrow(anti_join(renewables_long, emissions, by = c("ISO", "Year"))),
    nrow(anti_join(consumption, emissions, by = c("ISO", "Year"))),
    nrow(anti_join(countries, emissions, by = "ISO"))
  )
)
kable(join_report, caption = "Rows that failed to match on each join")

# Which countries are behind the unmatched rows?
master %>%
  group_by(ISO, Country) %>%
  summarise(NoRenewables = all(is.na(RenewMatch)),
            NoConsumption = all(is.na(ConsMatch)),
            NoCountryInfo = all(is.na(CtryMatch)), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(NoRenewables | NoConsumption | NoCountryInfo) %>%
  print(n = 30)

master <- select(master, -RenewMatch, -ConsMatch, -CtryMatch)
```

*How many rows failed to match on each join, and what did you do about
them?*

After the 5 duplicate rows were removed, the master data frame built
from Emissions.csv contained 3,000 rows, covering 150 countries over 20
years. Each of the three sources was attached with a left join, so every
master row was kept and no rows were added.

The Renewables join, which used the ISO codes mapped from country names
in 1.2 together with Year, left 80 master rows unmatched. All of them
belong to 4 countries that have no row in Renewables.csv (4 countries ×
20 years). In the other direction, no renewables row was left unused,
which shows that the name mapping in 1.2 successfully matched every
remaining country.

The Consumption join, on ISO and Year, left 1,103 master rows from 56
countries unmatched. Most of these come from 55 countries that have no
consumption-based data at all (55 × 20 = 1,100 rows); the remaining 3
rows are years missing from one country's otherwise complete record.
Again, no row of Consumption.csv went unused. This confirms that
trimming and upper-casing the ISO codes (for example " gha" to "GHA") in
1.3 and standardising the Year formats in 1.4 fixed every join failure
those defects would otherwise have caused. The Countries join, on ISO
alone, matched every master row.

I kept the unmatched rows in the master rather than dropping them,
because removing them would delete those countries' emissions from every
total in Task 2. Instead, their missing values were filled in Task 1.6,
and flag columns (RenewImputed and ConsImputed) record which countries'
values were imputed so that they can be identified in later analysis.

### 1.6 Handle the NAs

```{r t1q6}
na_before <- colSums(is.na(master))

master <- master %>%
  group_by(ISO) %>%
  arrange(Year, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    # Record coverage before anything is filled in.
    ConsImputed = all(is.na(ConsCO2)),
    RenewImputed = all(is.na(Renewables)),
    # Annual series change smoothly, so gaps inside a country's record
    # (including the negative/spike values set to NA) are interpolated.
    CO2 = InterpolateWithin(Year, CO2),
    OilCO2 = InterpolateWithin(Year, OilCO2),
    Renewables = InterpolateWithin(Year, Renewables),
    ConsCO2 = InterpolateWithin(Year, ConsCO2)
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    # A country whose CO2 is missing in every year cannot be recovered.
    CO2 = replace_na(CO2, 0),
    # DECISION: a country with no consumption data at all is assumed
    # trade-neutral (ConsCO2 = CO2, so NetImported = 0) rather than 0,
    # which would make it look like a huge carbon exporter (see 1A iii).
    ConsCO2 = if_else(is.na(ConsCO2), CO2, ConsCO2),
    # No renewable data at all: 0, flagged by RenewImputed.
    Renewables = replace_na(Renewables, 0),
    # Oil emissions cannot exceed the total after interpolation.
    OilCO2 = pmin(replace_na(OilCO2, 0), CO2)
  )

# Static variables: derive one from the other two where possible ...
master <- master %>%
  mutate(GDP = coalesce(GDP, GDPCapita * Population / 1e6),
         GDPCapita = coalesce(GDPCapita, GDP * 1e6 / Population))

# ... otherwise use the region median (one value per country, so large
# regions are not weighted by their number of rows).
region_medians <- master %>%
  distinct(ISO, Region, Population, GDPCapita) %>%
  group_by(Region) %>%
  summarise(MedPop = median(Population, na.rm = TRUE),
            MedGDPCapita = median(GDPCapita, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")

master <- master %>%
  left_join(region_medians, by = "Region") %>%
  mutate(PopImputed = is.na(Population),
         Population = coalesce(Population, MedPop),
         GDPCapita = coalesce(GDPCapita, MedGDPCapita),
         GDP = coalesce(GDP, GDPCapita * Population / 1e6)) %>%
  select(-MedPop, -MedGDPCapita)

tibble(Variable = names(na_before),
       NA_before = na_before,
       NA_after = colSums(is.na(master))[names(na_before)]) %>%
  filter(NA_before > 0) %>%
  kable(caption = "Missing values before and after treatment")

cat("Countries with consumption imputed as CO2:",
    n_distinct(master$ISO[master$ConsImputed]), "\n")
cat("Countries with no renewables data (set to 0):",
    n_distinct(master$ISO[master$RenewImputed]), "\n")
cat("Countries with population from the region median:",
    n_distinct(master$ISO[master$PopImputed]), "\n")
```

*Justify your treatment of each variable. Different variables may
warrant different choices.*

The 4 missing CO2 values are the negative figures removed in 1.4b, and
the 5 missing OilCO2 values are -999 missing-value codes (for example
Qatar 2016 and Zimbabwe 2010); each is listed in the defect log. I
filled them by linear interpolation from the same country's neighbouring
years. Annual emissions change gradually and each gap is a single year,
so interpolation produces a realistic estimate, whereas replacing them
with 0 would understate CumCO2 in every subsequent year.

Renewables had 84 missing values, which needed two different treatments.
Four of them are Romania's blank cells for 2015 to 2018, which I
interpolated between its 2014 value (27.12 TWh) and its 2019 value
(24.63 TWh). The other 80 belong to the 4 countries with no renewables
data at all. Because there is no country-specific value to interpolate
from, I set these to 0 and flagged them with RenewImputed. I chose this
over a regional average, which would invent generation that these
countries may not have, while accepting that `Renew_PC` will be
understated for any of them that do generate renewable electricity.

`ConsCO2` had the largest gap, with 1,105 missing values. For the 55
countries with no consumption data at all, I assumed trade neutrality by
setting ConsCO2 equal to CO2, so their NetImported is 0, and recorded
this with ConsImputed. Setting them to 0 instead would claim that these
countries consume no emissions whatsoever, making NetImported equal to
-CumCO2 and presenting every one of them as a large exporter of embodied
carbon, a bias examined in 1A iii. The remaining gaps, the country
missing 3 years and Panama's two implausible values (0.28 in 2007 and
0.17 in 2011, against a typical value of about 3.7), were interpolated
within each country's own series.

GDP and GDPCapita each had 500 missing values, from 25 countries, such
as Aruba and Andorra, that have neither figure, so one could not be
derived from the other. I filled GDPCapita with the median of its
region, calculated from one value per country so that regions were not
weighted by their number of rows, and then calculated GDP as GDPCapita ×
Population / 1e6. This keeps each country's real population in its GDP
estimate and keeps the three columns mathematically consistent. Dropping
these countries would remove their emissions from every total, and using
0 would distort the correlations and models in Task 3.

Population had no missing values. Its only defect, Chile's recorded
population of 19,553, had already been corrected in 1.4b to the value
implied by its GDP and GDPCapita.

### 1.7 Add `Decade` and `Period`

```{r t1q7}
master <- master %>%
  mutate(
    Decade = paste0(Year %/% 10 * 10, "s"),
    Period = factor(if_else(Year < 2016, "Pre-Paris", "Post-Paris"),
                    levels = c("Pre-Paris", "Post-Paris"))
  )

count(master, Decade, Period)
```

### 1.8 Add the four cumulative variables

*`CumCO2`, `CumOilCO2`, `CumRenew`, `CumConsCO2`.*

```{r t1q8}
# Running totals must be computed within each country, in year order.
master <- master %>%
  arrange(ISO, Year) %>%
  group_by(ISO) %>%
  mutate(CumCO2 = cumsum(CO2),
         CumOilCO2 = cumsum(OilCO2),
         CumRenew = cumsum(Renewables),
         CumConsCO2 = cumsum(ConsCO2)) %>%
  ungroup()

# Check: one country's first rows.
master %>%
  filter(ISO == first(ISO)) %>%
  select(Country, Year, CO2, CumCO2, Renewables, CumRenew) %>%
  head(5)
```

### 1.9 Add `NetImported` and `OilShare`

```{r t1q9}
master <- master %>%
  mutate(NetImported = CumConsCO2 - CumCO2,
         # Guard against division by zero for a country with no emissions.
         OilShare = if_else(CumCO2 > 0, CumOilCO2 / CumCO2, 0))

summary(select(master, NetImported, OilShare))
```

### 1.10 Add the four per-capita variables

*`CO2_PC`, `OilCO2_PC`, `Renew_PC`, `ConsCO2_PC`.*

```{r t1q10}
# Emissions are in million tonnes, so * 1e6 / Population gives tonnes per
# person. For renewables (TWh), * 1e6 / Population gives TWh per million
# people.
master <- master %>%
  mutate(CO2_PC = CumCO2 * 1e6 / Population,
         OilCO2_PC = CumOilCO2 * 1e6 / Population,
         Renew_PC = CumRenew * 1e6 / Population,
         ConsCO2_PC = CumConsCO2 * 1e6 / Population)

summary(select(master, CO2_PC, OilCO2_PC, Renew_PC, ConsCO2_PC))
```

```{r t1-check}
# A quick look at the finished master data frame.
dim(master)
glimpse(master)
cat("Remaining NAs:", sum(is.na(master)), "\n")
```

\newpage

## 1A. Data Quality Audit Report

*Approximately 250 words in total across the three parts below. Every
claim must reference a specific value, country, year or column from
**your** data.*

### i. Defect inventory

```{r t1a-detection}
# Evidence used for detection: summary() of the numeric columns before any
# fix (impossible minima, extreme maxima) ...
summary(select(emissions_before_fix, CO2, OilCO2))
summary(select(countries_raw %>%
                 mutate(across(c(popData2022, GDP, `GDP/capita`),
                               ToNumber)),
               popData2022, GDP, `GDP/capita`))

# ... and the defect log built step by step in Task 1 (detection and
# handling text is shown in full in the table below).
defect_log %>%
  filter(Rows > 0) %>%
  select(File, Column, Rows, Example) %>%
  kable(caption = "Defect log (generated from the detection code)")
```

| File | Column | Rows affected | Example (country, year) | How I detected it | How I handled it |
|------------|------------|------------|--------------|------------|------------|
| Emissions.csv | All columns | 5 | Maldives 2008; Sierra Leone 2016 | `duplicated()` across every column returned TRUE | Removed with `distinct()` |
| Emissions.csv | `annual_co2_mt` (CO2) | 4 | Sri Lanka 2012 (-3.645); Sweden 2022 (-2.594) | `summary()` showed a minimum of -3.645, which is physically impossible; `filter(CO2 < 0)` listed the rows | Set to NA, then interpolated from neighbouring years |
| Emissions.csv | `annual_oil_co2_mt` (OilCO2) | 5 | Bosnia and Herzegovina 2007; Qatar 2016 (-999) | `summary()` showed a minimum of -999; exact match to the missing-value code | Set to NA, then interpolated |
| Consumption.csv | `Country Code` (ISO) | 76 (50 countries) | " are" (United Arab Emirates) 2014 | Failed the three-capital-letter regex but passed after `str_trim()` + `str_to_upper()` | Trimmed and upper-cased |
| Consumption.csv | `Year` | 114 | United Arab Emirates "FY2004", "01/01/2009", "2010.0" | `ClassifyYearFormat()` count table showed four formats | Converted to integer with `ParseYear()` (lubridate for dates) |
| Consumption.csv | `Consumption CO2` | 5 | China 2018 ("9,443.433") | `str_detect(value, ",")`: thousands separator stored as text | Separator removed by `ToNumber()` |
| Consumption.csv | `Consumption CO2` | 2 | Panama 2007 (0.28); Panama 2011 (0.17) | `FlagSpikes()`: below one-tenth of Panama's median (3.718) | Set to NA, then interpolated |
| Consumption.csv | `Year` (missing years) | 3 | Panama 2006, 2008, 2016 | Join report: one country with 3 unmatched country-years | Interpolated within Panama's series |
| Consumption.csv | Whole file (coverage) | 55 countries (1,100 master rows) | Aruba, Afghanistan, Angola (all years) | Join report: no Consumption row for these ISO codes | `ConsCO2 = CO2`, flagged `ConsImputed` (see iii) |
| Countries.csv | `popData2022` (Population) | 1 | Chile 2022 (19,553) | `Population` differed from `GDP * 1e6 / GDPCapita` (ratio 0.001) | Replaced with implied population (19,553,317) |
| Countries.csv | `GDP`, `GDP/capita` | 25 countries (500 master rows) | Aruba 2022; Andorra 2022 | NA count in the 1.6 missing-value table | Region-median GDPCapita; GDP derived from it |
| Renewables.csv | `Country.Region` | 2 rows (40 country-years) | World 2004; European Union (27) 2004 | No match in the name lookup; aggregate keyword | Removed (would double-count countries) |
| Renewables.csv | `Country.Region` | 6 names (120 country-years) | United States of America 2004; Burma 2004 | Name absent from Emissions `location` after normalisation | Mapped with `name_fixes` |
| Renewables.csv | Year columns | 4 | Romania 2015–2018 | `is.na(Renewables)` after pivoting: blank cells | Interpolated between 2014 (27.12) and 2019 (24.63) |
| Renewables.csv | Coverage | 4 countries (80 master rows) | See the 1.5 join report | Join report: 80 master rows unmatched | Set to 0, flagged `RenewImputed` |

Most defects were mechanical (duplicates, formats, keys, separators) and
could be repaired without loss. The substantive ones (negative CO2, -999
codes, Chile's population) were found by testing values against physical
or arithmetic limits, not by inspection.

### ii. The negative emissions problem

```{r t1a-negatives}
# The negative rows, the value before treatment, and the value now in the
# master after interpolation from neighbouring years.
negative_rows %>%
  rename(CO2_original = CO2) %>%
  left_join(select(master, ISO, Year, CO2_imputed = CO2),
            by = c("ISO", "Year")) %>%
  kable(caption = "Negative annual CO2 rows", digits = 2)

# Context: two years either side of each negative value.
negative_rows %>%
  select(ISO, NegYear = Year) %>%
  inner_join(select(emissions_before_fix, ISO, Country, Year, CO2),
             by = "ISO", relationship = "many-to-many") %>%
  filter(abs(Year - NegYear) <= 2) %>%
  select(Country, Year, CO2) %>%
  kable(caption = "Neighbouring years", digits = 2)
```

*Which rows are they? Why do negative values legitimately appear in
published emissions series? What did you do, and what alternative did
you reject?*

Four rows in Emissions.csv record negative annual emissions: Equatorial
Guinea in 2010 (-0.995 Mt), Sri Lanka in 2012 (-3.645 Mt), Sudan in 2018
(-1.256 Mt) and Sweden in 2022 (-2.594 Mt). Negative values do appear
legitimately in published series in two situations. The first is a
genuine removal of carbon from the atmosphere, for example when a
country's forests or other land-use sinks absorb more CO2 than it emits,
giving negative net emissions. The second is an accounting revision:
when a previously published estimate is corrected downward, a series
recording annual changes or corrections can show a negative entry even
though nothing was physically removed. Neither applies here.
annual_co2_mt measures production-based emissions, which contain no
sinks, and each negative value sits between ordinary positive years;
Sweden, for example, emitted 38.568 Mt in 2021 and 36.709 Mt in 2023.
These rows are therefore data errors. I set them to NA and interpolated
from the neighbouring years, giving Sweden 2022 a value of about 37.64
Mt. This keeps each country's cumulative total realistic. I rejected
taking the absolute value: it would replace Sweden's 2022 figure with
2.594 Mt, still around 93% below its neighbours, so flipping the sign
corrects the sign but not the size.

### iii. Coverage gap in consumption-based data

```{r t1a-coverage}
no_cons <- master %>%
  filter(ConsImputed) %>%
  distinct(ISO, Country)
n_no_cons <- nrow(no_cons)
cat("Countries with no consumption-based data:", n_no_cons, "of",
    n_countries, "\n")
cat("Examples:", paste(head(no_cons$Country, 3), collapse = ", "), "\n")

last_year_preview <- filter(master, Year == max(Year))

# Do covered and uncovered countries differ?
last_year_preview %>%
  group_by(Coverage = if_else(ConsImputed, "No consumption data",
                              "Has consumption data")) %>%
  summarise(Countries = n(),
            MedianPopulation_m = median(Population) / 1e6,
            MedianGDPCapita = median(GDPCapita),
            MedianCumCO2 = median(CumCO2),
            MedianCO2_PC = median(CO2_PC),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  kable(digits = 1, caption = "Covered vs uncovered countries")

# What real covered countries look like: NetImported as a share of CumCO2.
last_year_preview %>%
  filter(!ConsImputed) %>%
  summarise(MinShare = min(NetImported / CumCO2),
            MedianShare = median(NetImported / CumCO2),
            MaxShare = max(NetImported / CumCO2)) %>%
  kable(digits = 3,
        caption = "NetImported / CumCO2 among countries with data")

# Counterfactual: what zero imputation would have produced instead.
# Zero gives NetImported = -CumCO2 (a share of -1) and ConsCO2_PC = 0.
zero_bias <- last_year_preview %>%
  filter(ConsImputed) %>%
  transmute(Country, CumCO2, CO2_PC,
            NetImported_zero = 0 - CumCO2,
            ConsCO2_PC_zero = 0,
            ConsCO2_PC_now = ConsCO2_PC) %>%
  arrange(NetImported_zero)

kable(head(zero_bias, 5), digits = 1,
      caption = "Most biased countries under zero imputation")
```

*How many countries have no coverage? Name three. Is imputing zero
valid? If it biases `ConsCO2_PC` and `NetImported`, in which direction,
and for which type of country is the bias worst? Support this with a
number.*

55 of the 150 countries in my Emissions.csv (37%) have no
consumption-based data at all, for example Aruba, Afghanistan and
Angola.

Imputing zero is not a valid strategy. A value of zero claims that a
country's population consumed no goods or energy with embodied
emissions, which is impossible. The data are missing, not zero. The
coverage gap is also not random: the uncovered countries have a median
population of 2.1 million against 16.1 million, a median GDP per capita
of 11,085 against 17,023, and a median CumCO2 of 32.1 Mt against 821.7
Mt. A zero would therefore distort one distinct group of countries
rather than add random noise.

Zero imputation biases both variables downward. ConsCO2_PC falls to 0
for every uncovered country, and NetImported becomes -CumCO2, a
NetImported/CumCO2 share of -1. That is twice as extreme as the largest
real net exporter among covered countries (a share of -0.49), and far
below their median of +0.15, which shows that the typical covered
country is a net importer. Every uncovered country would wrongly appear
as an extreme exporter of embodied carbon.

The bias is worst for uncovered countries with large production-based
emissions, which are typically fossil-fuel producers. In absolute terms,
NetImported would be understated by the full cumulative total: 2,898.4
Mt for Algeria and 2,889.6 Mt for Iraq. Per person, ConsCO2_PC would
fall from 158.0 t to 0 for Libya and from 136.5 t to 0 for Serbia. I
therefore imputed ConsCO2 = CO2 (trade-neutral, NetImported = 0)
instead, while recognising that, if the covered countries' median share
of +0.15 also holds for these countries, this still slightly understates
their consumption.

# Task 2: Exploratory data analysis

### 2.1 Highest-emitting year, and the largest year-on-year fall

```{r t2q1}
yearly_totals <- master %>%
  group_by(Year) %>%
  summarise(TotalCO2 = sum(CO2), Countries = n_distinct(ISO),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(Year) %>%
  mutate(Change = TotalCO2 - lag(TotalCO2),
         PctChange = 100 * Change / lag(TotalCO2))

peak_year <- slice_max(yearly_totals, TotalCO2, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
largest_fall <- slice_min(yearly_totals, Change, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

cat("Highest total CO2:", peak_year$Year, "with",
    comma(peak_year$TotalCO2, accuracy = 0.1), "Mt\n")
cat("Largest year-on-year fall:", largest_fall$Year, "(",
    comma(largest_fall$Change, accuracy = 0.1), "Mt,",
    round(largest_fall$PctChange, 2), "%)\n")

# The Countries column confirms the fall is not caused by countries
# dropping out of the record that year.
kable(yearly_totals, digits = 1)
```

*What caused the largest fall?*

Total emissions peaked at 34,067.6 Mt in 2023, and the largest fall was
in 2020 (-1,329.5 Mt, -4.04%), which I attribute to the COVID-19
pandemic, when lockdowns sharply cut transport and industrial fuel use.
The fall is not a coverage artefact, since all 150 countries report in
every year, and its temporary nature fits a pandemic shock: emissions
rebounded by 1,538.9 Mt in 2021, the largest rise after 2010's recovery
from the only other notable fall (-371.8 Mt in 2009, during the global
financial crisis).

### 2.2 Cumulative totals over time for the whole dataset

```{r t2q2, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
cum_totals <- master %>%
  group_by(Year) %>%
  summarise(across(c(CumCO2, CumOilCO2, CumConsCO2, CumRenew), sum),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_longer(-Year, names_to = "Measure", values_to = "Value") %>%
  mutate(
    # Emissions (Mt) and renewables (TWh) have different units, so they
    # get separate panels rather than one misleading shared axis.
    Panel = if_else(Measure == "CumRenew", "Renewable generation (TWh)",
                    "Emissions (Mt CO2)"),
    Measure = recode(Measure, CumCO2 = "Production CO2",
                     CumOilCO2 = "Oil CO2",
                     CumConsCO2 = "Consumption CO2",
                     CumRenew = "Renewables")
  )

ggplot(cum_totals, aes(Year, Value, colour = Measure)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ Panel, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "Cumulative emissions and renewable generation, all countries",
       x = "Year", y = "Cumulative total", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

*Observation:* by 2023 the 150 countries had emitted 606,423.7 Mt of
production-based CO2 since 2004, with consumption-based emissions
(597,745.8 Mt) tracking almost the same path, which is expected since
trade only moves emissions between countries. Oil accounts for 30.3%
(184,040.5 Mt) of the total. The renewables curve bends upward, unlike
the near-straight emissions lines, showing that annual renewable
generation grew faster over the period than annual emissions.

## 2A. Counterintuitive finding

*What did you expect, and why was that reasonable?*

I expected the countries with the largest cumulative emissions to also
lead the per-capita ranking, and expected any per-capita leaders outside
that group to be oil-dominated economies. This was reasonable because a
handful of large industrial economies dominate the totals (China alone
emitted 184,474.9 Mt, 30% of the sample), and oil is the fuel most
associated with high-consumption lifestyles and petro-states.

*What does the data actually show? Quote a specific value, country or
trend from your own plots.*

Only two countries, the United States (320.5 t per person) and Saudi
Arabia (357.3 t), appear in both `top10total` and `top10percap`. The
per-capita leader is Qatar at 588.8 t per person, 4.5 times China's
129.4 t and 20 times India's 28.7 t, despite having just 2.9 million
people and a cumulative total (1,703.1 Mt) under 1% of China's. Only 3
of the top 10 per-capita countries have more than 10 million people. The
supporting chart also contradicts the second half of my expectation:
Qatar, Bahrain, Brunei and the United Arab Emirates sit at the top-left
in dark colours, meaning oil makes up under a quarter of their
cumulative emissions, while the oil-dominated (yellow) points are mostly
small island economies such as Aruba.

*What real-world mechanism could explain the discrepancy?*

Two mechanisms combine. The first is population size: per-capita
emissions divide a country's total by its population, so a country with
fewer than 3 million people needs only a modest industrial base to post
a very high figure. The second is energy resource endowment combined
with production-based accounting. Qatar, Bahrain, Brunei and the UAE are
natural-gas exporters: liquefying and processing gas, refining,
petrochemicals and energy-intensive industries such as aluminium
smelting, all powered by cheap domestic gas, emit CO2 inside their
borders, even though much of the output is exported and consumed
elsewhere. Production-based accounting assigns all of those emissions to
a small resident population, which is why gas, not oil, drives the
highest per-capita figures.

### Supporting visualisation

```{r t2a-plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
# Population vs per-capita emissions, coloured by oil share: tests whether
# the per-capita leaders are small, oil- or gas-intensive economies rather
# than the large total emitters.
label_iso <- union(top10total$ISO, top10percap$ISO)

ggplot(lastYear_data, aes(Population / 1e6, CO2_PC)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = CumCO2, colour = OilShare), alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_text(data = filter(lastYear_data, ISO %in% label_iso),
            aes(label = Country), size = 2.8, vjust = -0.9,
            check_overlap = TRUE) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(labels = label_percent()) +
  scale_size_continuous(labels = label_comma(), range = c(1, 10)) +
  labs(title = "Small populations, high per-capita emissions",
       x = "Population (millions, log scale)",
       y = "Cumulative CO2 per capita (t, log scale)",
       colour = "Oil share", size = "Cumulative CO2 (Mt)")
```

*Caption (2–3 sentences): what does this chart show, and why did you
choose this chart type?*

Each point is one country in 2023, placed by population and cumulative
CO2 per person, with bubble size showing its cumulative total and colour
its oil share. The per-capita leaders cluster at the top-left (small
populations), while the largest total emitters (the biggest bubbles,
China and India) sit at the right with moderate per-capita values. I
chose a scatter plot with log axes because population ranges from
thousands to 1.4 billion and per-capita emissions from under 1 to 589 t,
and size and colour let one chart test both parts of the explanation.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2B. Visualisation design critique

**Visualisation chosen:** Question 2.6, cumulative CO2 over time for the
top 10 countries (log y-axis).

The first design decision was the log scale. Cumulative totals range
from 10,360.2 Mt (Indonesia) to 184,474.9 Mt (China); on a log axis,
equal vertical distances are equal ratios, so all ten growth paths are
readable and comparable. The second was labelling each line at its end
instead of using a legend, so a reader does not have to match ten
colours. I rejected a linear y-axis: China and the United States would
fill the plot while the other eight countries collapsed into an
indistinguishable band near zero, hiding the fact that India overtook
Japan and Russia, which matters to a climate-policy audience tracking
emerging emitters. The limitation is that the log scale shrinks gaps:
China's lead over Indonesia is about 18 times, but the lines look close.
A reader could also mistake the steep early rise for an emissions surge
when it is the running total starting in 2004. I would mitigate both
with an annotation stating the ratio and a subtitle explaining that the
totals start in 2004.

# Task 3: Data-driven modelling

### 3.1 Build `cor_data`

```{r t3q1}
# Final-year record for each country (each country's own last year, in
# case a country's record ends early). Country names are kept as row
# names so the diagnostic plots in 3A label points by country.
cor_data <- master %>%
  group_by(ISO) %>%
  filter(Year == max(Year)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(Country, CumCO2, CumConsCO2, Population, GDP, GDPCapita) %>%
  column_to_rownames("Country") %>%
  as.data.frame()

dim(cor_data)
head(cor_data)
```

### 3.2 Correlation matrix

```{r t3q2, fig.width=6, fig.height=5}
cor_matrix <- cor(cor_data)
round(cor_matrix, 2)

as.data.frame(as.table(cor_matrix)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(Var1, Var2, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", Freq)), size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166AC", mid = "white", high = "#B2182B",
                       limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Correlation matrix of cor_data", x = NULL, y = NULL,
       fill = "r") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

cor_gdp <- cor(cor_data$CumCO2, cor_data$GDP)
cor_gdp_pc <- cor(cor_data$CumCO2, cor_data$GDPCapita)
cat("cor(CumCO2, GDP)       =", round(cor_gdp, 2), "\n")
cat("cor(CumCO2, GDPCapita) =", round(cor_gdp_pc, 2), "\n")
```

*Report `cor(CumCO2, GDP)` and `cor(CumCO2, GDPCapita)`. Why are those
two numbers so different?*

`cor(CumCO2, GDP)` is 0.98 and `cor(CumCO2, GDPCapita)` is 0.12. They
differ because GDP and cumulative emissions are both measures of *size*:
they grow with a country's population and total economic activity, so
the same few giants (China, the United States, India) top both. GDP per
capita removes size and measures wealth per person, which on its own
says little about total emissions: rich but small countries such as
Luxembourg and Singapore have small totals, while populous middle-income
countries such as China (GDP per capita 18,921) and India (7,350) have
the largest.

### 3.4 Train/test split

```{r t3q4}
## Required — do not remove or change this line:
set.seed(seed_from_id(params$studentID))

# Your 65/35 split goes below.
train_idx <- sample(seq_len(nrow(cor_data)),
                    size = round(0.65 * nrow(cor_data)))
train_data <- cor_data[train_idx, ]
test_data <- cor_data[-train_idx, ]

cat("Training rows:", nrow(train_data), "| Testing rows:", nrow(test_data),
    "\n")
```

### 3.5 Linear model: `CumCO2 ~ GDP`

```{r t3q5}
model_gdp <- lm(CumCO2 ~ GDP, data = train_data)
summary(model_gdp)

pred_gdp <- predict(model_gdp, newdata = test_data)
rmse_gdp <- Rmse(test_data$CumCO2, pred_gdp)
r2_gdp <- RSquared(test_data$CumCO2, pred_gdp)
cat("Test RMSE (GDP only):", round(rmse_gdp, 2), "Mt | Test R2:",
    round(r2_gdp, 3), "\n")
```

### 3.6 Linear model: all predictors

```{r t3q6}
model_full <- lm(CumCO2 ~ CumConsCO2 + Population + GDP + GDPCapita,
                 data = train_data)
summary(model_full)

pred_full <- predict(model_full, newdata = test_data)
rmse_full <- Rmse(test_data$CumCO2, pred_full)
r2_full <- RSquared(test_data$CumCO2, pred_full)
cat("Test RMSE (all predictors):", round(rmse_full, 2), "Mt | Test R2:",
    round(r2_full, 3), "\n")
```

### 3.7 Interpret and compare the two models

*When should the first be preferred, and when the second? If the full
model has the higher test RMSE, explain why — that is not an error.*

On the 52 test countries, the full model clearly outperforms the
GDP-only model: its test RMSE is 647.46 Mt against 1,719.84 Mt, and its
test R² is 0.973 against 0.812. In my split, the model with more
predictors therefore does *not* have the higher test RMSE. Its advantage
comes almost entirely from `CumConsCO2`, which correlates 0.99 with
`CumCO2`. This is close to target leakage: consumption-based emissions
are production-based emissions adjusted for trade, and for the 55
countries without consumption data `CumConsCO2` was set equal to
`CumCO2` in Task 1.6, so the model partly learns an identity.

The GDP-only model should be preferred when the aim is explanation or
when consumption data are unavailable. It is easy to interpret: each
additional million dollars of GDP is associated with 0.00616 Mt (about
6,200 t) more cumulative CO2 since 2004. Its single coefficient is also
stable, whereas the full model's coefficients are distorted by
multicollinearity: GDP receives a *negative* coefficient (-0.0052 Mt per
million dollars) and GDPCapita is not significant (p = 0.342), because
GDP and `CumConsCO2` carry almost the same information (r = 0.99).

The full model is better for pure prediction when every predictor,
including genuine consumption-based data, is available for the country
being predicted.

Had the full model's test RMSE been higher, that would not have been an
error: extra correlated predictors can overfit the 98 training countries
and generalise worse, and with only 52 test countries a single large
emitter can swing the RMSE.

### 3.8 Alternative models

```{r t3q8}
predictors <- c("CumConsCO2", "Population", "GDP", "GDPCapita")
x_train <- as.matrix(train_data[, predictors])
x_test <- as.matrix(test_data[, predictors])
y_train <- train_data$CumCO2
y_test <- test_data$CumCO2

# Cross-validation folds are random; seeding again makes the lambda
# choice reproducible. The train/test split above is unaffected.
set.seed(seed_from_id(params$studentID))

# Ridge (alpha = 0) and lasso (alpha = 1); lambda chosen by 5-fold CV
# (5 rather than 10 folds because the training set is small).
ridge_cv <- cv.glmnet(x_train, y_train, alpha = 0, nfolds = 5)
lasso_cv <- cv.glmnet(x_train, y_train, alpha = 1, nfolds = 5)
pred_ridge <- as.numeric(predict(ridge_cv, newx = x_test,
                                 s = "lambda.min"))
pred_lasso <- as.numeric(predict(lasso_cv, newx = x_test,
                                 s = "lambda.min"))
coef(lasso_cv, s = "lambda.min")  # which predictors lasso keeps

# Regression tree, pruned at the complexity with lowest CV error.
tree_fit <- rpart(CumCO2 ~ ., data = train_data, method = "anova",
                  control = rpart.control(minsplit = 6, cp = 0.001))
best_cp <- tree_fit$cptable[which.min(tree_fit$cptable[, "xerror"]), "CP"]
tree_pruned <- prune(tree_fit, cp = best_cp)
pred_tree <- predict(tree_pruned, newdata = test_data)

# Log-log linear model: addresses the skew seen in 3.3 and 3A.
# log1p() keeps zero values defined; predictions are back-transformed.
model_log <- lm(log1p(CumCO2) ~ log1p(CumConsCO2) + log1p(Population) +
                  log1p(GDP) + log1p(GDPCapita), data = train_data)
pred_log <- expm1(predict(model_log, newdata = test_data))

model_comparison <- tibble(
  Model = c("Linear (GDP only)", "Linear (all variables)",
            "Ridge (all variables)", "Lasso (all variables)",
            "Regression tree", "Log-log linear (all variables)"),
  RMSE = c(rmse_gdp, rmse_full, Rmse(y_test, pred_ridge),
           Rmse(y_test, pred_lasso), Rmse(y_test, pred_tree),
           Rmse(y_test, pred_log)),
  R_squared = c(r2_gdp, r2_full, RSquared(y_test, pred_ridge),
                RSquared(y_test, pred_lasso), RSquared(y_test, pred_tree),
                RSquared(y_test, pred_log))
) %>%
  arrange(RMSE)

kable(model_comparison, digits = 3, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
      caption = "Test-set performance (RMSE in Mt CO2)")
```

The log-log linear model performs best (test RMSE 577.66 Mt, R² 0.979),
because modelling every variable on a log scale removes the extreme
right skew of `CumCO2` (3.3) so that a few giants no longer dominate the
fit. The plain full linear model is second (647.46 Mt). Regularisation
did not help: lasso (985.15 Mt) and ridge (1,089.57 Mt) shrink
coefficients towards zero, which costs accuracy when there are only four
predictors and a strong signal. Lasso's coefficients are informative,
though: it dropped GDP entirely and kept `CumConsCO2` (coefficient
1.03), confirming that GDP adds nothing once consumption emissions are
known. The regression tree is worst (2,075.52 Mt, R² 0.726): its
predictions are piecewise constant, and with only a handful of very
large countries in 98 training rows it cannot represent the extreme
values that dominate RMSE.

## 3A. Assumption checking

### i. Linearity

```{r t3a-linearity, fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
train_long <- train_data %>%
  rownames_to_column("Country") %>%
  pivot_longer(all_of(predictors), names_to = "Predictor",
               values_to = "Value")

# Solid line: linear fit. Dashed line: flexible (loess) fit. Where the two
# diverge, a straight line is a poor description of the relationship.
ggplot(train_long, aes(Value, CumCO2)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, span = 0.9,
              colour = "firebrick", linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ Predictor, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "CumCO2 against each predictor (training data)",
       x = "Predictor value", y = "Cumulative CO2 (Mt)")

# Pearson measures linear association, Spearman monotonic association; a
# large gap between them signals a non-linear relationship.
train_long %>%
  group_by(Predictor) %>%
  summarise(Pearson = cor(Value, CumCO2),
            Spearman = cor(Value, CumCO2, method = "spearman"),
            Gap = Spearman - Pearson, .groups = "drop") %>%
  kable(digits = 3)
```

*Does a linear relationship look reasonable? Which predictor departs
from it most clearly?*

A linear relationship looks reasonable for `CumConsCO2` and `GDP`: the
linear and loess fits nearly coincide, and the Pearson correlations
(0.995 and 0.983) match the Spearman rank correlations (0.988 and
0.947). This fit is largely driven by a few very large countries,
though, with most countries bunched near the origin. `GDPCapita` departs
from linearity most clearly: its linear correlation is only 0.105, but
its rank correlation is 0.533, a gap of 0.429, so richer countries do
tend to emit more but not in a straight line. `Population` also curves
visibly, because China and India have similar populations but very
different emissions.

### ii. Distribution of the response

```{r t3a-normality}
# Numerical support for the 3.3 histograms: a strongly right-skewed
# variable has a mean far above its median.
c(Mean = mean(train_data$CumCO2), Median = median(train_data$CumCO2))
shapiro.test(train_data$CumCO2)
shapiro.test(log1p(train_data$CumCO2))
```

*Using your plots from 3.3 — does raw `CumCO2` satisfy the normality
assumption? Is a transformation warranted?*

No. The raw histogram in 3.3 puts almost every country in the first bin,
with a long right tail out to China (184,474.9 Mt). In the training data
the mean (5,312.5 Mt) is almost 15 times the median (362.2 Mt), and the
Shapiro–Wilk test rejects normality decisively (W = 0.236, p \<
2.2e-16). On the log scale the histogram is roughly symmetric and the
test no longer rejects normality (W = 0.994, p = 0.947), so a log
transformation is warranted. Strictly, the assumption applies to the
residuals rather than the response, but a response this skewed produces
skewed residuals, as the Q–Q plot in iii confirms.

### iii. Residual diagnostics

```{r t3a-diagnostics, fig.width=8, fig.height=7}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(model_full, which = c(1, 2, 3, 5))
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

| Plot | What assumption it tests | Does your model satisfy it? |
|----------------------|------------------------|---------------------------|
| Residuals vs Fitted | Linearity: residuals should scatter randomly around 0 at every fitted value | No: the red line curves upward, with China's residual far above 0 and the United States' at about -5,800 |
| Normal Q-Q | Normality of the residuals: points should follow the diagonal | No: both tails leave the line, with China above +5 and India and the United States below -5 standardised residuals |
| Scale-Location | Constant variance (homoscedasticity): the line should be flat | No: the line rises steeply from about 0.5 to 2.5, so the error spread grows with the size of the country |
| Residuals vs Leverage | Influential observations: no point should lie beyond the Cook's distance contours | No: China (leverage 0.785), India (0.772) and the United States (0.678) lie beyond the Cook's distance 1 contour, against a threshold of 0.102 |

### iv. Influential observations

```{r t3a-leverage}
# Leverage (hat value) and Cook's distance for each training country.
# Rule of thumb: leverage above 2p/n is high.
p <- length(coef(model_full))
n <- nrow(train_data)
influence_tbl <- tibble(Country = names(hatvalues(model_full)),
                        Leverage = hatvalues(model_full),
                        CooksD = cooks.distance(model_full)) %>%
  arrange(desc(Leverage))

cat("High-leverage threshold (2p/n):", round(2 * p / n, 3), "\n")
kable(head(influence_tbl, 5), digits = 3)

high_lev_country <- influence_tbl$Country[1]
cat("High-leverage country:", high_lev_country, "\n")

model_full_drop <- lm(CumCO2 ~ CumConsCO2 + Population + GDP + GDPCapita,
                      data = train_data[rownames(train_data) !=
                                          high_lev_country, ])
rmse_full_drop <- Rmse(test_data$CumCO2,
                       predict(model_full_drop, newdata = test_data))
cat("Test RMSE with", high_lev_country, "removed:",
    round(rmse_full_drop, 2), "Mt (was", round(rmse_full, 2), "Mt)\n")
```

**High-leverage country:** China (leverage 0.785, Cook's distance 37.65)

**New test RMSE without it:** 546.71 Mt (down from 647.46 Mt)

*Is removing it defensible? Two sentences.*

Removing China is not defensible as data cleaning, because its values
are genuine: it is the world's largest emitter (184,474.9 Mt), and a
model that excludes it cannot describe the country that matters most for
emissions policy. The lower test RMSE only shows that China was bending
the fit for typical countries, a problem better addressed by the log
transformation (577.66 Mt with China kept) than by deletion, unless
China is explicitly modelled and reported separately.

### v. Verdict

*Is linear regression a valid choice here? If assumptions are violated,
what does that mean in practice for your coefficients and predictions?*

Linear regression on the raw scale is not a valid choice for inference
here: all four diagnostics fail, and the fit is dominated by three
countries. In practice, the standard errors and p-values in 3.6 cannot
be trusted. The reported p \< 2e-16 for GDP overstates certainty, and
GDP's negative coefficient reflects multicollinearity with `CumConsCO2`
(r = 0.99), not a real effect, so individual coefficients should not be
interpreted. Predictions are also unreliable for typical countries: the
test RMSE of 647.46 Mt is larger than the median training country's
entire cumulative total (362.2 Mt), so relative errors for small
countries are huge, and prediction intervals assuming constant variance
would be far too narrow for large countries. The model is usable only as
a rough predictor for large emitters. A log-log specification, which
improved the test RMSE to 577.66 Mt and makes the response approximately
normal (W = 0.994), is the better choice.
